strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2f36d5f96e484b0a909e1a74482bdc70/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents an interesting, reasonably original synthesis of rank-one eigensystem updates, hierarchical graph partitioning, and spectral GNNs. The exact factorization viewpoint is potentially useful beyond the proposed architecture.

The exposition gives useful intuition for progressively merging local spectral representations. Deflation for repeated eigenvalues and update directions orthogonal to eigenspaces is discussed, addressing an important technical complication omitted by simpler rank-one-update treatments.

The synthetic timing experiments support the expected qualitative dependence on graph size and interface size, while the four heterophily benchmarks indicate that the model can attain competitive predictive performance with relatively few learned parameters.

The paper acknowledges unfavorable large interfaces, approximation through aggressive sparsification, and the transductive scope of the experiments. The application appears low-risk, with no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central complexity theorem is not established as stated. Appendix E derives an additional O(k^2 n(L^2 log n-L^3)) term and then drops it when declaring O(kn^2) without assumptions under which it is dominated. Algorithm 2 also constructs and stores dense Cauchy matrices, but memory, forward-pass cost, and the practical realization of the cited fast Cauchy products are not analyzed. Thus the headline quadratic-complexity claim is materially underqualified.

There is a serious theory-to-experiment mismatch: the rank-one edge-update derivation applies to the combinatorial Laplacian, whereas experiments use the normalized Laplacian. Adding an edge changes the degree normalization, so the normalized Laplacian is not obtained by the same fixed-coordinate rank-one update. The assertion that everything applies identically through a D^{-1/2} change of basis is insufficient and generally does not provide an orthogonal eigendecomposition or the claimed update sequence.

The interface-sparsification theorem and proof are inconsistent. The theorem gives O(n log n/epsilon^2) edges, while the proof claims O(epsilon^{-2}) edges per interface; standard sparsification bounds depend on the number of incident vertices. The claimed O(n log n) construction also suppresses accuracy and solver costs. Experimentally retaining as few as one crossing edge is not shown to satisfy the stated spectral guarantee.

The claimed O(epsilon) stability of arbitrary Lipschitz spectral filters does not follow directly from quadratic-form approximation: scalar Lipschitz continuity alone is generally insufficient for an operator bound between noncommuting Laplacians. No empirical approximation-error measurement checks this claim under the extreme 99–99.5% interface sparsification used in experiments.

The empirical evidence is too limited for the architectural claims. There are only four transductive datasets, no ablations for local filters, hierarchy, partition choice, sparsification level, or number of levels, and no accuracy-versus-runtime/memory comparison. Reported timing covers preprocessing only, rather than end-to-end training and inference. The numerical Global-GFT results and parameter counts underlying Figure 4 are not tabulated, and no significance tests support statements of superiority.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or repository is supplied; random seeds, model-selection protocol, optimizer details such as weight decay, Euler step size, exact filter construction, numerical secular solver settings, and provenance or retuning of baseline results are missing. Algorithm 3 is incomplete for the final secular root because it refers to an undefined lambda_{n+1}, and it does not implement the deflation required by the theory.

Presentation is generally readable, but important notation is inconsistent: Lemma 3.1 and Theorem D.1 disagree on a leading sign, and the main text versus Appendix B alternates between U(Phi) and U(Phi)^T in the forward transform. Figure 4 is too small to verify its quantitative claims, and the Grad-CAM node-attribution procedure for node classification is underspecified and does not by itself establish interpretability.

Overall, the factorization idea has promise, but unsupported complexity and normalized-Laplacian claims affect the paper's central soundness rather than being minor omissions. Substantial theoretical correction and broader, reproducible evaluation are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: The core idea—constructing a hierarchical GFT from rank-one edge updates and inserting learnable filters between local Cauchy factors—is interesting and reasonably original. The rank-one update perspective is mathematically natural, and the attempt to handle repeated eigenvalues through deflation is valuable.
The synthetic experiments qualitatively support dependence on graph size and interface size, while the real-data results show that the model can remain competitive after substantial sparsification.
The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished, with useful diagrams, pseudocode, dataset statistics, and some dataset-specific hyperparameters.
The application has no evident major societal or ethical risk.
weaknesses: The central complexity guarantee is not established as stated. Appendix E derives an additional O(k^2 n(L^2 log n-L^3)) term and then drops it without an assumption under which it is dominated by O(kn^2). The analysis also invokes an O(n log n) Cauchy matrix-vector product while Algorithm 3 explicitly constructs a dense n-by-n matrix; the required fast, stable implementation is neither specified nor evaluated.

The sparsification theory is internally inconsistent with the implemented method. Theorem 4.1 states k'=O(n log n/epsilon^2), its proof instead claims O(epsilon^-2) edges per interface, and the asserted O(n log n) construction time omits dependence on the input edge count and epsilon. Experiments retain fixed fractions as small as 0.5%, producing interfaces of one edge, but provide no evidence that these graphs satisfy the claimed spectral-approximation guarantee.

The normalized-Laplacian experiments do not clearly follow from the combinatorial-Laplacian derivation. Adding an edge changes the degree normalization, whereas Algorithm 2 always uses sqrt(w)(e_u-e_v). The statement that the factorization transfers 'identically' through a D^-1/2 change of basis is insufficient because this is a congruence rather than an orthogonal eigendecomposition. Sparsifying the combinatorial graph also changes the normalization used downstream.

The claimed O(epsilon) stability of arbitrary Lipschitz spectral filters is insufficiently justified. Relative quadratic-form approximation alone does not generally control eigenvectors without eigengap assumptions, and scalar Lipschitz continuity is not by itself enough for the asserted matrix-function bound.

The formal development contains consequential gaps and inconsistencies. Theorem D.1 is effectively asserted from prior restricted results rather than fully proved; its proof appears to reverse the empty/nonempty affected-set cases. Algorithm 3 references the undefined interval (lambda_n,lambda_{n+1}), does not implement the required deflation, and the orientation of U(Phi) differs between the main formulation and Appendix B.

The evaluation is too limited to support the broad claims. It covers only four transductive node-classification datasets and uses only one hierarchy level in real experiments. There are no ablations for partition choice, hierarchy depth, sparsification rate, local filters, or shared parameters; no factorization residual or spectral-error measurements; and no accuracy-versus-epsilon analysis.

The runtime comparison reports preprocessing only, not end-to-end training/inference time, memory, or per-layer application cost. It is also unclear whether direct eigendecomposition and the factorization operate on the same sparsified Laplacian, which is essential for a fair comparison. Leaf eigendecomposition costs remain material with the shallow real-data partition.

Empirical gains are overstated. L2G-Net is clearly compelling mainly on Minesweeper; it trails Polynormer on three of four datasets and GRAMAGCN on Tolokers, while several differences from spectral baselines are small relative to reported variation. Parameter efficiency does not substitute for missing compute and memory comparisons.

The Grad-CAM cumulative-contribution plot does not establish interpretability or a beneficial locality bias. Concentrated attribution is not necessarily faithful, and no attribution fidelity, stability, or task-performance tradeoff is measured.

Reproducibility is inadequate without code and complete training/model-selection details. Missing items include seeds, validation and checkpoint-selection procedures, hyperparameter-search spaces, Euler step size, weight decay, nonlinearities, exact filter definitions, actual parameter counts, and a stable fast-Cauchy implementation.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering numerical conditioning of secular equations and Cauchy factors, dependence on interface size and favorable partitions, aggressive topology alteration, shallow-hierarchy costs, transductive scope, and sensitivity near repeated or clustered eigenvalues. These unresolved soundness and evidential issues prevent acceptance despite the promising idea.

strengths: Originality: The local-to-global construction is conceptually interesting. Expressing a graph Fourier basis through hierarchical rank-one eigen-updates and inserting learnable filters between the resulting Cauchy factors offers a distinctive connection between numerical linear algebra and spectral GNN design.

Significance: If made rigorous and implemented efficiently, the framework could reduce the preprocessing cost of exact spectral methods on graphs with genuinely small hierarchical interfaces while providing a useful structural inductive bias.

Presentation: The main motivation and high-level architecture are communicated clearly, with a helpful overview figure and a generally well-organized progression from factorization to graph partitioning and learning.

Empirical promise: L2G-Net is competitive on the four heterophily benchmarks, uses substantially fewer learned parameters than Polynormer, and the synthetic timing curves qualitatively support quadratic scaling in graph size and linear scaling in the retained interface size.
The appendix discusses repeated eigenvalues and update directions through deflation, gives pseudocode, reports dataset-specific hyperparameters, and includes a broad baseline table.
weaknesses: Soundness: The interface-sparsification result is not established as stated. The theorem gives k'=O(n log n/epsilon^2), while its proof claims O(epsilon^-2) edges per interface; the latter does not follow from standard spectral sparsification. Its asserted O(n log n) construction time also omits dependence on the input edge count and epsilon. Most importantly, the experiments retain as few as one crossing edge, but no evidence shows that this extremely sparse interface satisfies the claimed spectral approximation.

Soundness: The claimed O(epsilon) perturbation of a spectral layer is asserted from scalar Lipschitz continuity of the filter. Loewner approximation of two Laplacians does not by itself yield this conclusion for arbitrary scalar-Lipschitz matrix functions with changing eigenvectors; stronger operator assumptions and a precise norm-dependent bound are needed.

Soundness and presentation: Sign and transpose conventions are inconsistent in central formulas. Definition 3.1 already places a minus sign in the affected Cauchy block, Lemma 3.1 states U_tilde^T=D U^T, but Theorem D.1 states U_tilde^T=-D U^T. Likewise, the main architecture uses U(Phi) where the appendix uses U(Phi)^T. These discrepancies leave the claimed exact factorization and implemented layer insufficiently specified.

Complexity: The appendix derives an additional update cost O(k^2 n(L^2 log n-L^3)) and then drops it from the final O(kn^2) bound without stating conditions under which it is dominated. It also invokes an O(n log n) Cauchy matrix-vector algorithm while Algorithm 3 explicitly forms a dense n-by-n Cauchy matrix. Numerical precision, storage complexity, forward-pass cost, and backward-pass cost are not analyzed.

Evidence: There is no numerical reconstruction or orthogonality-error experiment demonstrating that the proposed factorization recovers eigenvectors accurately, especially under repeated or tightly clustered eigenvalues. Runtime alone cannot validate the central exactness and numerical-stability claims.

Evaluation: The real-data study uses only four transductive datasets and a single two-way partition, so it does not test the proposed multilevel hierarchy. It lacks ablations for partition choice, hierarchy depth, sparsification ratio, local filter placement, and exact versus sparsified factorization, as well as end-to-end training/inference time and memory comparisons.

Significance of results: The method is clearly best only on Minesweeper, by 0.04 AUC over Polynormer, which is well within the reported run-to-run variation. It trails the strongest method on the other three datasets. Thus the results support competitiveness and parameter efficiency, but not broad performance superiority.

The Grad-CAM experiment does not substantiate interpretability: concentrated attribution is not necessarily more faithful or understandable, and the manuscript provides no faithfulness test or sufficient detail about adapting Grad-CAM to transductive node classification.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or executable implementation is provided, and important training and model-selection details are missing. The reported hyperparameters are helpful but insufficient to reproduce the factorization, numerical solver, architecture, and evaluation protocol reliably.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges transductive evaluation and unfavorable dense interfaces in passing, but lacks a consolidated discussion of numerical stability, memory, graph-specific preprocessing, sensitivity to sparsification, and failure modes. Ethical risk is low for this methodological work, but the consequences of topology-altering sparsification for biased or minority subpopulations are not considered. Overall, the promising core idea is outweighed by unresolved errors in central guarantees and insufficient validation, preventing acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper presents an interesting connection between hierarchical graph decompositions, rank-one eigensystem updates, and Cauchy-like factors. Using this structure to insert learnable local filters between successive merges is a novel and potentially useful spectral-GNN design.

Presentation: The high-level local-to-global motivation is clear, the paper is visually polished, and the main architecture is explained with helpful diagrams, algorithms, and comparisons to message passing, graph transformers, and conventional spectral filtering.

Empirical scope: Evaluation spans synthetic scaling tests, four heterophilous graphs, two inductive molecular benchmarks, and four very large city graphs. L2G-Net is competitive on several tasks and particularly strong on Minesweeper, while using fewer learned parameters than transformer baselines.

The authors provide useful implementation details, including dataset-specific hyperparameters, partitioning and sparsification procedures, hardware, seed counts, training times, and memory estimates. They also honestly acknowledge quadratic scaling and that linear-time message-passing or polynomial methods remain preferable in some large-scale regimes.
Research ethics: The work presents no evident material ethical concern. The generic impact statement is adequate for this primarily algorithmic contribution.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 4.1 appears false as stated. It claims that every interface can be spectrally sparsified to O(epsilon^-2) edges, independent of the number of incident vertices. Standard spectral-sparsification bounds depend on the number or effective rank of vertices, and an interface containing many independent bridge directions (for example, a matching, with arbitrarily weak internal edges if connectivity is required) cannot generally be preserved multiplicatively with a constant number of edges. This invalidates the claimed route from arbitrary graphs to bounded-cut HGFs and the assertion that the preprocessing guarantees the advertised complexity.

The central complexity claim is internally inconsistent. Theorem 3.2 states sequential complexity O(k n^2 + sum_i f_i(n)), linear in k, but Appendix F derives an additional O(k^2 n(L^2 log n-L^3)) term for a fast Cauchy product and O(k^2 n^2) when dense products are used. The appendix then drops this term based on empirical behavior rather than a bound. Thus the advertised O(k n^2) theorem is not established for variable k.

The implementation/storage model is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 2 explicitly constructs a dense s-by-s Cauchy matrix, whereas Section 6.6 asserts that storing one costs O(s), presumably through an implicit generator representation. The paper does not explain how the reported implementation applies and stores all factors, reconciles this with Algorithm 2, or maintains numerical stability. Memory values are therefore difficult to verify.

The claimed exact large-scale spectral processing is misleading: the city experiments retain only two cut edges between subgraphs, so the factorization is exact only for a heavily sparsified graph, not for the original graph. No reconstruction error, spectral-approximation error, downstream accuracy-versus-sparsification curve, or comparison against the unsparsified factorization is reported.

The normalized-Laplacian experiments are not adequately connected to the theory. Adding an edge changes degree normalization, so it is not directly a rank-one update between normalized Laplacians. A valid construction might keep the final degree scaling fixed and factor a sequence of intermediate symmetric matrices, but neither the algorithm nor proof specifies this. The brief statement that normalization is merely a change of basis is not sufficient to justify exactness.

The proof of the foundational progressive identity is too cursory for the claimed generalization: Appendix E largely asserts the result after deflation, contains confusing handling of the affected set S and sign conventions, and does not rigorously establish the repeated-degeneracy construction. Since exactness is the main theoretical contribution, this needs a complete proof and numerical reconstruction validation.

Experimental evidence does not adequately isolate the proposed ingredients. There are no ablations over hierarchy depth, partition strategy, cut size, sparsification ratio, local versus global filters, or implicit Cauchy implementation. The synthetic timing comparison uses dense numpy.linalg.eigh, only three repetitions, and no factorization-error measurement; very-large-graph eigendecomposition times are extrapolations rather than observations.

The predictive gains are generally modest: the method leads clearly only on a subset of tasks, is below the best method on most heterophily and peptide results, and is often comparable within reported variability. Claims about interpretability based on Grad-CAM concentration are also not validated against explanation fidelity or stability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied hyperparameters: no code or artifact availability is stated, key numerical solver and implicit-factor details are missing, the hyperparameter-selection protocol is unspecified, and several reported claims such as parameter efficiency are presented graphically without complete numerical accounting.

Overall, the architectural idea is promising, but unsupported or contradictory claims about interface sparsification, complexity, exactness, and storage affect the paper's central contribution rather than a peripheral detail. These issues prevent reliable acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The central idea—using rank-one Laplacian updates and Cauchy-like eigenbasis transformations to organize spectral computation hierarchically—is interesting and appears meaningfully original in the GNN context. It connects classical divide-and-conquer eigensolvers with graph partitions in a potentially useful way.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. It provides intuition, pseudocode, proofs, hyperparameters, runtime measurements, memory estimates, and experiments spanning synthetic, transductive, and inductive settings.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark. L2G-Net is competitive on several heterophilous and long-range datasets, uses relatively few learnable parameters, and clearly outperforms the reported global-GFT baseline. The authors also honestly acknowledge that linear-time message passing or polynomial filters remain preferable in strictly large-scale regimes.
The work has low apparent direct ethical risk, and no material research-ethics concern is evident from the applications considered.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.1, which is central to extending the favorable complexity claim to arbitrary graphs, appears false. It asserts that every interface can be spectrally sparsified to O(epsilon^-2) edges independent of the interface size. Standard sparsification bounds depend on the number of vertices, and an interface consisting of many independent bridge edges cannot preserve its quadratic form for epsilon<1 after retaining only a constant number of edges. Independently sparsifying interfaces also does not establish the claimed global (1±epsilon) bound as written. Consequently, the claimed bounded-cut reduction for arbitrary graphs is unsupported.

The proof of Theorem 3.2 does not establish its stated O(k n^2) complexity. Appendix F derives additional O(k^2 n(L^2 log n-L^3)) or O(k^2 n^2) terms, then replaces them with O(k n^2) based on an empirical observation that not all updates touch the same subgraph. An observed typical behavior cannot prove the worst-case theorem. The assumed near-linear Cauchy multiplication is also cited without specifying its numerical accuracy, implementation, or constants.

The manuscript repeatedly blurs exact processing of the original graph with exact factorization of a sparsified graph. City-Networks retains only two bridge edges per subgraph pair, so the resulting transform is exact only for a substantially modified graph. No spectral distortion, factorization residual, downstream sensitivity to sparsification, or accuracy-versus-cost curve is reported, yet the text calls this 'exact spectral processing.'

Most derivations and pseudocode concern combinatorial-Laplacian rank-one edge updates, whereas key experiments use the normalized Laplacian. Adding an edge changes node degrees, so a sequential normalized-Laplacian update is not immediately the rank-one operation analyzed. The brief claim that normalization requires only a change of basis does not specify a fixed-degree construction or show that Algorithm 3 implements it. This leaves a theory–experiment gap.

Other mathematical statements are insufficiently justified or inconsistent. The spectral-bisection cost is given as O(|E|2^L), but with L=log n this is O(|E|n), not 'nearly linear.' Theorem 5.1 states strict containment for every eligible graph, while its proof supplies only one two-node example and an informal generalization. There is also a sign discrepancy between Lemma 3.1 and Appendix Theorem E.1.

The empirical gains do not compensate for these central soundness problems. On the four Platonov datasets, L2G-Net is clearly best only on Minesweeper and the margin there is within reported variability; it trails Polynormer on the other three. City-Networks gains are modest, and peptides-struct trails several simpler competitors. Important ablations are absent, including hierarchy depth, partition choice, local versus global filters, sparsification strength, and parameter- or compute-matched comparisons.

Reproducibility is inadequate for validating the strongest claims. No code or artifact is identified; the partition search and cost function f(G) are not fully specified; the stated theoretical epsilon is disconnected from the empirical retention ratios; and numerical stability is not evaluated despite chaining secular solves and applying a 1e-12 deflation threshold. Reported eigengaps are not a substitute for eigenvalue, orthogonality, or factorization-residual errors.

The limitations discussion acknowledges cut dependence and quadratic scaling but does not confront the invalid sparsification bound, the approximation introduced by aggressive edge removal, or numerical stability. The generic impact statement is acceptable for this low-risk work, but it provides little substantive analysis. Overall, the potentially valuable idea requires major theoretical correction and substantially stronger validation before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper proposes an interesting connection between hierarchical graph partitions, rank-one Laplacian updates, Cauchy-like matrices, and spectral GNNs. Turning this factorization into a local-to-global architecture is conceptually appealing and could be useful for long-range graph learning.

Soundness: The exact rank-one-update factorization for the combinatorial Laplacian is developed with definitions, algorithms, deflation for repeated eigenvalues, and an expressiveness result showing that the proposed operator class strictly contains global spectral filters.

Evaluation: The experiments cover synthetic scaling, heterophilous transductive datasets, inductive molecular benchmarks, and very large city graphs. L2G-Net is generally competitive, uses relatively few learned parameters, and the paper reports preprocessing, training-time, and memory comparisons.

Presentation: The motivation and high-level construction are clear, figures are helpful, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges the quadratic regime, unfavorable large cuts, and settings where message passing remains preferable.
Ethics: The work concerns general graph-learning methodology and raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 4.1 appears false as stated. It claims that every interface can be spectrally sparsified to O(epsilon^-2) edges, independent of interface size. General spectral sparsification requires a number of edges depending on the number or rank of involved vertices; an interface consisting of many independent matching edges cannot preserve all Laplacian quadratic forms after being reduced to a constant number of edges. The proof merely invokes standard sparsification and does not establish this much stronger result. This theorem is central to extending the favorable complexity claim to arbitrary graphs.

Soundness: The theory is derived from rank-one updates of the combinatorial/generalized Laplacian, but key experiments use the normalized Laplacian. Adding an edge changes the degree normalization, so the normalized Laplacian is not generally modified by a single rank-one update. Appendix A's statement that the factorization applies identically up to a D^-1/2 change of basis does not resolve the fact that D changes during successive updates. Consequently, the exactness of the implemented normalized-Laplacian factorization is not established.

Complexity: The headline O(k n^2) theorem is not supported by Appendix F. That appendix derives additional terms involving k^2 and states that dense Cauchy multiplication gives O(k^2 n^2), recovering O(k n^2) only as an empirical observation. It also invokes O(n log n) Cauchy multiplication without specifying the approximation, tolerance, numerical guarantees, or implementation. Algorithm 2 explicitly constructs a dense n-by-n Cauchy matrix. These discrepancies undermine the central scalability claim.

Claims and evidence: After cut sparsification, the method exactly processes the sparsified graph, not the original graph. The manuscript nevertheless repeatedly describes the large-scale experiments as exact spectral processing. The asserted O(epsilon) layer-output error is not proved under the actual learned filter parameterization, normalized Laplacian, and multi-layer nonlinear network.

Evaluation: There is no direct numerical validation that the factorized transform matches a conventional eigendecomposition, especially under degeneracy, normalized Laplacians, and sparsification. Important ablations are also missing: accuracy versus sparsification ratio/error, hierarchy and partition choices, number of levels, and alternative partitions. Projected cubic eigendecomposition times are not a substitute for comparison with scalable partial or structured eigensolvers.

Reproducibility: No code or implementation link is provided. Several decisive details remain unclear, including how Cauchy products are represented and evaluated at large scale, solver tolerances and numerical stability, construction of the claimed confidence intervals, baseline tuning, and actual end-to-end resource use on the 100k-569k-node graphs. The reported large-graph factorization results are therefore difficult to independently verify.

Presentation: The paper is polished at a high level, but several internal inconsistencies need resolution—for example, Section 6.4 says two edges are retained between each subgraph pair whereas Table 8 reports dataset-dependent sparsification ratios, and the main theorem statements omit qualifications that appear in the appendix. Because the unsupported results underpin the paper's main efficiency and generality claims, these are acceptance-blocking issues rather than minor revisions.
